title: Cartloads of books
hookLine: read cartloads of books, but only one thing counts; all else is ego's talk (Asa di Var, ang 467)

lines: A LIST OF BOOKS TO READ.
cards: A list of books to read someday. Podcasts saved for later. Tabs opened and never closed.
It's a strange modern condition: drowning in things to know, and still unsure of the main thing. Guru Nanak lived when a book was copied by hand, a precious object.
And still he pictured someone with so many books they had to be hauled away in carts. Then he asked what all of it was worth.

teach.b: The salok is on ang 467, and its pictures pile up on purpose. In paraphrase: you could read and read and fill whole carts with books. You could read and load caravans.
You could read and fill boats, and fill pits. You could read for years and years, every month of the year, your whole life, with every breath. And then the last line drops like a stone.
Nanak, only one thing is counted. Ik gal. Everything else is ego's babble.
Gal is everyday Punjabi for a thing, a matter, a word said. Only one matter goes into the account. What is it?
The salok doesn't spell it out in that line, but Sikh teachers read it as the Name, remembering the One, lived in the heart. And notice what Guru Nanak doesn't say.
He doesn't say reading is bad. The Gurus were poets and scholars.
Sikh tradition credits Guru Angad with shaping the Gurmukhi script and teaching people to read it. Gurdwaras read from the Guru Granth Sahib every day. The point is what reading is for.
Learning that only makes a bigger pile, a bigger I who knows more, is yesterday's ego in a new outfit.

Learning that leads to one thing, lived, is something else. The very next salok says it sharply: the more one writes and reads, the more one burns. Set beside this salok, the burning is learning that only feeds the self.
There's relief in this. You don't have to get through the whole pile. You only have to let one line actually change you.

how: Sikhs read and sing Gurbani daily, and this salok of Asa di Var, sung at dawn, reminds them that reading is meant to lead to remembering the One, not to a pile of knowledge.

o: the one thing that is counted

games.why: Nanak, only one thing is counted. Sikh teachers read it as the Name, remembered and lived.

practice: Choose one line you've met on this path, maybe today's, only one thing is counted, and say it slowly, once. Say it again and stop on each word; notice which one catches, and if your mind rushes on, come back to the one line.
If you pray, say Waheguru between the repetitions.

wordCard.voice: Ik gal, one thing, one matter: Guru Nanak's picture of endless reading, carts, caravans and boats of it, says only ik gal is counted; the rest is ego's talk.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: one thing, one matter; gal is everyday Punjabi for a thing said or a matter.

carryVoice: Your line: one thing counts. You don't have to finish the pile. Day five hundred forty-seven, done.
